title: Why Pineapple Digests Your Tongue (pH 3 Acid Helps) 🍍
description:
Why does pineapple make your tongue sting? Bromelain, a mix of protein-cutting enzymes in fresh pineapple, breaks down the slimy mucus coat in your mouth, and the fruit's acid then stings the exposed spots. Heat changes the enzyme's shape, which is why canned or grilled pineapple doesn't bite.

topic: Why does pineapple make your tongue sting?
script: Pineapple digests your tongue with every bite you take. That sting on your tongue, isn't just sour. Pineapple is packed with bromelain, a mix of enzymes that chop up protein. And your tongue? It's made of protein. So while you're chewing, bromelain cuts into the slimy coat, that protects your mouth. Then the fruit's acid, around pH three to four, splashes onto the exposed spots. That's the sting. Meat tenderizer powders often use the same enzyme, so yes, your tongue is getting tenderized. But heat changes the enzyme's shape, at about seventy to eighty degrees Celsius, and it stops working. That's why canned or grilled pineapple doesn't bite. Relax, your mouth heals fast, tiny damage can fade within hours. So tell me, would you still eat a fruit that digests your tongue?
key_facts: Bromelain is a mix of protein-cutting enzymes found in pineapple; it breaks down the mucous lining and surface tissue of the mouth (Science Meets Food, Science ABC).
Acid intensifies the sting by hitting freshly exposed tissue; pineapple is about pH 3 to 4 (Science ABC, Inverse).
Powdered meat tenderizers often contain bromelain or papain (Science Meets Food).
Heat denatures bromelain; about 70 to 80 C (160 to 175 F) tames it, and canned pineapple has been heated (Inverse, Science Meets Food).
Mouth tissue heals fast; trivial damage heals within hours (Science ABC).
